Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is furniture because whole physical-object token resolves the asset as furniture. Model it as a human-scale furniture, fixture, workstation, storage, sanitary, or interior-use asset with credible ergonomics, supports, joinery, and a clear use case. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Seat or work height, depth, back angle, leg clearance, storage volume, support placement, and reachable controls must immediately explain how a person uses the object. Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starstop Snack Shelf; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Model load-bearing frames, legs, pedestals, brackets, seams, cushions, panels, drawers, hinges, plumbing, glides, cable routing, fasteners, wall anchors, or floor anchors appropriate to the item. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Place it on a named floor, wall, counter, workstation, classroom, bedroom, shop, restaurant, sanitary, storage, or service socket. Feet, wall brackets, plumbing, cable routes, backs, and user clearance must align with the room and nearby interaction positions. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Preserve seats, drawers, doors, screens, lamps, cushions, controls, storage, plumbing fixtures, and movable surfaces as distinct objects when gameplay can sit, open, use, move, customize, or damage them. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Keep ergonomic silhouette and contact points at every LOD. Repeated slats, legs, buttons, cushions, shelves, and fasteners should share meshes or instances. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Seat or work height, depth, back angle, leg clearance, storage volume, support placement, and reachable controls must immediately explain how a person uses the object.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starstop Snack Shelf is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

materialPlan.metalRule: Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material.
materialPlan.glassRule: Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane.
materialPlan.masonryRule: Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling.
materialPlan.woodRule: Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use.
materialPlan.flexibleRule: Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling.
materialPlan.emissiveRule: Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure.

interactionAndAnimation.guidance: Keep access panels, doors, lights, propulsion units, controls, cargo areas, steering surfaces, lift hardware, and service interfaces separately named for animation, customization, damage, maintenance, and gameplay states.

Studio/backlot.” A production-ready Studio Set Wall Modular, designed as a specialized asset awaiting a dedicated family builder for Starline City. Do not create a generic primitive substitute. Keep the item queued as unsupported until a purpose-built family generator exists. The object must remain immediately recognizable from silhouette and required components, use physically coherent construction and human or vehicle scale, and follow the town direction: glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. This asset appears under the blueprint section “D. Studio/backlot” and should visibly support that gameplay or environmental role rather than acting as generic filler. The blueprint evidence is: C. Roads and street props D. Studio/backlot

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is generic_prop because no stronger physical category was found, so the asset remains a generic prop. Model it as a production-ready environmental or interactive prop with a recognizable purpose, coherent assembly, correct scale, and town-specific materials. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: The primary body and functional secondary parts must identify the object before labels or color. Handles, supports, openings, controls, edges, and contact points should explain use. Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Studio Set Wall Modular; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Model the load-bearing body, panels, seams, hinges, fasteners, supports, handles, vents, feet, brackets, openings, service access, and functional hardware appropriate to the object. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Place it on a named ground, wall, ceiling, counter, shelf, dock, room, vehicle, terrain, water, or gameplay socket appropriate to its use. Every foot, base, root, bracket, anchor, contact edge, and suspension point must sit flush or visibly explain how it is supported. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Separate parts that may open, rotate, light, display, receive an item, emit particles, take damage, change material, or connect to another system. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve silhouette and interaction points, sharing repeated hardware and moving only microdetail into materials at lower LODs. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: The primary body and functional secondary parts must identify the object before labels or color. Handles, supports, openings, controls, edges, and contact points should explain use.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Studio Set Wall Modular is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

materialPlan.woodRule: Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use.
materialPlan.flexibleRule: Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling.
materialPlan.emissiveRule: Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure.
